back: The dissociation curve moves right at higher partial pressure of CO₂, so haemoglobin releases oxygen more readily.

front: Why is the Hb dissociation curve S-shaped?
back: Cooperative binding: first O₂ changes Hb's shape, making further binding easier; the last site is harder to fill.
Plateau at lung pO₂: full loading. Steep at tissue pO₂: large release for a small fall.
(saturation leaving lungs − saturation leaving tissue) ÷ 100 × oxygen capacity.
CO₂ + H₂O → H₂CO₃ (carbonic anhydrase) → H⁺ + HCO₃⁻; HCO₃⁻ out to plasma, Cl⁻ in (chloride shift); H⁺ + Hb → HHb.
Hydrogencarbonate ions (about 85%), carbaminohaemoglobin, dissolved in plasma.
Movement of chloride ions into red blood cells to balance hydrogencarbonate ions leaving.
To the left of adult Hb: higher affinity, so it takes O₂ from maternal blood in the placenta.
One haem; hyperbolic curve far to the left; oxygen store released at very low pO₂.
